Critically, no alternative diagnosis (e.g., DRESS, AGEP, EM major, pemphigus) explains *concurrent full-thickness epidermal necrosis on biopsy*, *mucositis*, *respiratory symptoms*, and *acute onset* — DRESS has latency >2–6 weeks, eosinophilia, and organomegaly (none reported); AGEP shows sterile pustules and dermal neutrophils, not necrosis; EM major lacks true epidermal detachment and has target lesions; autoimmune blistering diseases show immunofluorescence abnormalities and autoantibodies (not mentioned). Thus, the preponderance of evidence points to a drug- or Mycoplasma-induced SJS/TEN spectrum disorder — and given the presence of *mucositis + respiratory symptoms + epidermal necrosis*, the most precise unifying diagnosis is **Stevens-Johnson Syndrome**, as TEN would require ≥30% BSA detachment (not stated; “early TEN” is speculative without %BSA quantification).

[EVIDENCE]  
- Acute rash onset <24 hours  
- Rash localized to upper back (classic initial site in SJS/TEN)  
- Histopathology confirms epidermal necrosis and detachment  
- Mucositis present (oral or other)  
- New cough suggesting respiratory mucosal involvement  
- No reported fever (consistent with Mycoplasma-triggered SJS)  
- Mildly elevated IgE (non-specific but reported in SJS)  
- Hypoalbuminemia (reflects systemic inflammation and capillary leak)  
- Elevated creatinine (may indicate early renal involvement or prerenal AKI)  
- Negative DLST and drug-specific IgE (expected in T-cell–mediated SJS/TEN)  

[GAPS]  
- Percentage of total body surface area (TBSA) with epidermal detachment (critical to distinguish SJS [<10%], SJS-TEN overlap [10–30%], vs. TEN [≥30%])  
- Presence/absence of Nikolsky sign (clinical sign of epidermal detachment)  
- Ophthalmologic exam findings (conjunctival erosion/ulceration supports SJS)  
- Mycoplasma pneumoniae PCR or serology results (pending per “rule out infection”)  
- Detailed medication timeline (exact start dates and durations of all drugs, especially high-risk agents like allopurinol, sulfonamides, NSAIDs, leflunomide)  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Stevens-Johnson Syndrome
